utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, good morning to you, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you and thank you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, I'm with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic and I'm about to sneeze.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of matters that I want to talk with you about very briefly. The first is with regard -- we need to go into private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were trying to work out a schedule that would make it possible for to us do the things we need to do in Banja Luka in preparation for the defence. And once we started putting it on calendars and so forth, it became clear that we -- that it would make a huge amount of sense, in fact almost necessary, that we be in Banja Luka through the 8th of October, which would interfere with the scheduled activities on the 3rd of October. I just want to say that we are at your disposal and will certainly -- at least one of us would certainly be here on that day if necessary. It would involve, you know, a rather expensive round trip travel from Banja Luka here and then back again; and if that's important, then we'll do that. I was wondering, however, if it might make sense to move that all until the 9th and do it then but whatever Your Honour chooses we will of course accept. But I just wanted to point out that that is kind of a problem in terms of trying to get the things done we need to get done. Whatever you want to do is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I don't know if you ever any comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't particularly, save for this. We will be asking for proper summaries of -- on the date that Your Honour has already appointed, which I think is the end of September, for Mr. Ackerman to complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not going to change for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Absolutely. I'm just hoping that Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham's trip to Banja Luka doesn't mean to say that we are going to be told that they don't know what witnesses they are calling at the end of September nor can they tell us what these witnesses are going to say. That's the only comment that I'd make if there is any plan to go to Banja Luka in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that we will have the summaries, the identification material, with regard to about the same percentage of witnesses that we will call that the Prosecution was able to provide us at the beginning of their case. I think that's probably around 60 or 70 per cent, and we will certainly be that far along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No doubt we will add some witnesses as we go along, just like they did but that's where we will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Striving towards equality of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, this is the one time where it's not equality of arms because the reason, as I think Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman know that there were witnesses added in because witnesses suddenly, as it were, came out of the wood work. Now, Mr. Ackerman has known all along what the case is that he's got to meet and Mr. Brdjanin no doubt knows what witnesses he wants to call. Your Honour, that's all I'm going to say at the moment. I don't wants to anticipate that there is going to be a problem about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No, I don't think so. Let's not make a causus belli out of it. Mr. Ackerman, again, I find it difficult to understand how all of a sudden it's only today that you realise that you need to be until the 8th of October in Banja Luka, when you knew all along, especially for the last month and a half at least if not more that on the 3rd of October we were scheduled to hand down the oral decision on the Rule 98 bis, so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can explain that -- I can't explain it. I can tell you how it happened. I'm not sure it's an explanation. Mr. Cunningham and I have been talking for several days about we need to sit down with a calendar and figure out our schedule between now and the start of the case, and part of that has to be built around some other things. We finally got around to doing that last night and that's when we realised that this was a problem. So we should have done it long before and it's a matter of negligence if nothing else on my part. And I admit that, Your Honour. It should have been done much earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad you admit it. However -- okay. We will shift, Mr. Roberts, please you need to revise the draft scheduling order that we agreed upon yesterday and move everything to the -- what's on the 3rd will be moved to the 9th, not, however, the deadline for the submission of the lists of witnesses and all that. And 9th is now a firm date. I don't want to be accused any further of almost bending backwards to accommodate the Defence any further, Mr. Ackerman. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can take it because Your Honour raised yesterday - Mr. Ackerman wasn't in court - that the start date with cross-examination of the two Prosecution experts remains as the 14th of October? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. And I would need to know from Mr. Ackerman if he can tell us how long he expects to hold Mr. Treanor and Mr. -- forgot his name now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Brown in cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- the schedule that we did last night shows a -- the cross-examination of the two experts on the 14th, 15th, 16th and 17th and the first Defence witness on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you need the full four days?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thank you. So anything further? No? Let's bring the witness in. And try to finish with this witness today, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've spoken to Mr. Ackerman. We think it's possible. I'm not 100 per cent sure but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not stop either of you. It's definite. If necessary we will continue tomorrow. But I think if we get over and done with today, it's better so that we are left with whatever needs to be thrashed tomorrow administratively in particular before we go into recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time you're not receiving interpretation in your own language, please let me know. You are about to start giving evidence in this trial against Radoslav Brdjanin, and I see that you have been briefed already. You're required before you start giving evidence to make a solemn declaration to the effect that you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in the course of your testimony. The text you're holding in your hand, so please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. The procedure here, sir, is quite a simple one and more or less identical to what you find in domestic jurisdictions. You're going to first to be first

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to you. And she will then be followed by Mr. Ackerman, who is the gentleman -- first gentleman to your left, who is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. If at any time you are asked a question that you feel you should be exempted from answering, either because it might expose you to some criminal proceedings or denigrate you or whatever, please let me know, and we will consider your objection and decide accordingly. Ms. Korner will first go ahead with her questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, good morning to you. Is your name Milorad Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Milorad Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you born on the 12th of March of 1959 in Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, but I was born in Banja Luka on that date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think you are by nationality a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dodik, before I go into a little detail as to your background, so it's clear, I think it's right that you have appeared at this Tribunal once before, when you testified in the hearing relating to the sentence of Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I was a witness for her defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And on this occasion, you are appearing as a result of a summons that was issued for you to appear in this trial. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: You mean during Mrs. Plavsic's trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, here, today.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I came in response to the summons issued to me and I consider myself to be a person who is neither a witness for the Defence or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, please, a little bit about your background. I think it's right that you became active in politics after graduating from the school of political science in Belgrade, in about 1985?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And between 1985, up until the multi-party elections in 1990, were you the president of -- described as local government, I don't know. Were you the president of the assembly in the municipality of Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was president of the executive council, which may be considered as a type of local government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In the period from 1988 until 1990. Before that, I held important positions locally in the community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us so the Court understands how far away is Laktasi from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres away from the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is the airport for Banja Luka actually in the municipality of Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Only a few kilometres away from the centre of Laktasi, say about 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in the 1990 multi-party elections, were you a member of the alliance of reformist forces? It was a party formed for the whole of the former Yugoslavia with its president being effectively the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Mr. Markovic, Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was a member of that party and I was a candidate on the list of that party for the Banja Luka district, or rather, my name was first on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in fact, were you elected to the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was elected as member of parliament. The only candidate for that region for that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell us briefly what was the political platform of the alliance of reformist forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This was a party that had as its main thrust the preservation of Yugoslavia, engaging all factors in the former Yugoslavia. It was a party that believed that only a peaceful solution could avoid national rifts and conflicts. We all knew that they could only lead to terrible destruction and loss of lives. As you said, the president of that party was Mr. Ante Markovic. I was a member of the republican board of that party for Bosnia-Herzegovina and president of the regional board of that party for Krajina. As a party, we supported the reformist course charted by the government of Ante Markovic. We thought that it was necessary to find a compromise in order to preserve Yugoslavia. At that time, a platform was proposed by the federal government regarding the survival of Yugoslavia. That is to say four or five functions were to remain common, inter alia the army, foreign policy, a joint monetary policy and a few other segments. However, one must bear in mind that at that time, especially before the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Croatia, the party of Mr. Tudjman, the HDZ, won the election. Mr. Milosevic was in power in Serbia, and when national parties came to the fore, especially the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the atmosphere became such that it became obvious that there would be a conflict but nobody knew what the intensity of this conflict would be. It should also be noted that the three parties after the elections in 1990 set up a joint government in Bosnia-Herzegovina I'm talking about the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, and for a year --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that. I just want to deal with your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. career and then we'll come back to the nationalist parties as a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we just go through your political career, thereafter, in October of 1991, did you and other members of your party resign from the party? That is the reformist alliance?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. A number of the members of this party, together with the then president, Mr. Kecmanovic, did so. We simply decided to go on working as independent MPs for a simple reason. Already then -- I mean, it should be noted that Mr. Ante Markovic had been dismissed at that time, that the party was not functioning in the territory of the whole of Yugoslavia, that in Bosnia-Herzegovina it became obvious that a number of members of that party who were also MPs espoused the concept of the disintegration of Yugoslavia and they supported the concept of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. I and that group of MPs disagreed with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at a copy of the letter that you and your fellow deputies sent, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be a new exhibit, P2456.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an undated letter probably a copy, but we look at the signatures, does it contain people who signed the letter, Dr. Kuzmanovic, the president, Dr. Dragan Kalinic, yourself, Mr. Micic and Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this letter. I remember this event, and I have just explained the reasons why I agreed with this letter, though I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then I don't think we need to take you through the contents of the letter, thank you very much. Now, thereafter, as I say, just to complete the -- your political career, did you continue to take part in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina even after the SDS deputies left in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that it was not that the SDS left. They continued working within the framework of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina but what happened in October or November was the formation of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I must say that I attended that meeting in Sarajevo at the time and I believed that under conditions of complete national homogenisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, one should undertake to devise a policy for the Serbian national core which would imply negotiating peaceful position and a peaceful settlement to any potential conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I attended that assembly meeting of the Serbian people. So it wasn't a formal abandoning of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It continued working until, I think, January or maybe later, of 1992. Of course, many did leave the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sometimes HDZ members walked out and then came back, and the assembly looked more like a public meeting place at which members of the coalition in Bosnia-Herzegovina presented their various views, all designed towards complete national homogeneity of all three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I must say that in those days, sometime around the middle of 1991, armed conflicts had already flared up in Croatia and this had a significant impact on what was happening in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself. In fact, that was the event that was dominant in all discussions in the assembly. On the one side were the SDA and the HDZ, which supported the secession of Croatia, and on the other was the SDS that wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And that was what happened in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just, as I say, very quickly try and finish off your career -- I don't mean finish off your career in that sense, just move through the evidence about it. Did you, in fact, attend the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina until January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then in 1996, did you found your own political party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, please, the name of your party.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The party's name was the party of Independent Social Democrats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that a party at the level of the Republika Srpska and also what is now, what's called the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The party has its representatives in Republika Srpska and in the federation. It has elected deputies. We are now in the opposition in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think then there were elections held in 1997; is that right, Mr. Dodik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When Mrs. Plavsic became the President of Republika Srpska and you yourself were the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. Mrs. Plavsic at the elections of 1996, the first post-war elections, became president, and in the course of 1997, in the summer, in August, she disbanded the assembly and thereby enabled extraordinary elections which took place, I think it was September or October 1997. And at those elections, the SDS won a majority and a coalition government was formed of which I became the president in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For how long did you remain the president of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: From the 18th of January, 1998, until the 11th of January, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you say, at present, your party is in opposition. But it 13 is is it right that very recently you've just been re-elected president of th

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe a month ago, just over a month ago, at a party assembly meeting, I was re-elected president of the party, which is now called the Association of Independent Social Democrats, because it has been joined by several other parties that were in existence and were our allies and now they have integrated with us to form one party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, then, please to - as you began to tell us about - the three nationalist parties as you've described them, that is the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. Immediately after the 1990 elections, were these parties cooperating together?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Even prior to the elections, there was visible cooperation, that is, prior to the multi-party election, the SDA and the HDZ cooperated openly. After the elections, those two parties together with the SDS formed the first multi-party government in Bosnia-Herzegovina and appointed their ministers in that government and they shared government at the local level, that is, at the level of the municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. While my party and some other smaller parties were then the opposition and they were -- in other words, they were not in power.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From your position as an independent or smaller party and then as an independent, were you able to observe the functioning of these particular parties during the period up until the conflict broke out in 1992 in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, it looked like the bursts of democracy in Bosnia-Herzegovina. All the leaders in power kept giving lip service to democracy that had finally come into being. They started performing their duties, as is normal in any state. And we all knew that, as well as those in power, that Bosnia-Herzegovina was very fertile soil for influence coming from the broader region, primarily the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So that at the very beginning of the work of that government, there was a lot of debate as to how it would continue to function. The leaders and presidents of all the republics and then provinces in the former Yugoslavia frequently changed places and discussed how things would look. And they had meetings almost weekly in various places which created a kind of psychosis among the people, especially in view of the fact that it proved impossible for them to come to any kind of agreement. The Slovenes clearly opted for separating from Yugoslavia. Croatia, after the victory of the HDZ, also took a clear stand regarding its wish to have an independent state, whereas beyond Milosevic's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. leadership insisted on the preservation of Yugoslavia. Bosnia-Herzegovina because of its ethnic mix, the mix of three peoples, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, later known as Bosniaks, normally was fertile soil for bringing pressure to bear from all sides. So that it was impossible to adopt a unified position as to what should be done next. The representatives of the government, primarily Mr. Izetbegovic who was president of the Presidency, said one thing but something quite different was happening on the ground, and this could be felt with regard to other leaders of national parties, that is, the SDS and the HDZ. This applied to them too. And the crisis reached a climax when the parliament was reviewing and taking a position on the decision of the Croatian assembly in June 1991 for Croatia to separate from the former Yugoslavia. On that occasion, a parliament session was held at which Mr. Izetbegovic as a member of the Presidency took the floor and supported this decision of the Croatian Sabor or assembly. It should be said that this was supported by his party and the HDZ of Bosnia as well of course, and representatives of the SDS and I personally I must say opposed such a decision because we felt this only worsened the situation. And that Bosnia-Herzegovina should have a position of its own on this matter rather than joining either side. But it was quite clear that this was an event in which the government formed after the multi-party elections definitely split and went each side going its own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, before we proceed, any time the witness is going beyond what you need, you have my authority to stop him and move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much, but I just wanted to let him finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, all that I'm concerned about - I think you started to tell us this already - was that the declaration of independence in Croatia I think caused each of the parties to polarise. Is that a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That was quite visible, as I have just described. After that, it was very difficult to hold a parliament session at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move, please, then, to the events in the autumn of 1991. But before doing that, were you aware in April of 1991 that something called the Association of Bosnian Krajina Municipalities was formed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I do know that such a community was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you to look, please, at a document which is already an exhibit, P8. This is a decision on the municipality of Laktasi joining the Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities, and it was apparently held on the 11th of April, 1991. And do you identify the stamp as the municipal assembly stamp from Laktasi?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is the stamp of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is that also the signature of Mr. Jovic, who was the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I don't know whether that is his signature, but Mr. Jovic was the president of the assembly at the time. I'm just not familiar with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you present when this decision was made by the assembly to join this community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I do know that this happened but I don't remember being present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to come back in a moment to the purpose of this organisation as you understood it, but that was April of 1991. Were you aware in September of 1991 that the Autonomous Region of Krajina assembly was created?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: About that time, there were attempts to form such an assembly. I do know -- I happened to be in Sarajevo at a parliament session and it was clear that a number of delegates were absent from the Banja Luka region. And we learnt that a meeting was being held in Grahovo. And I know that Karadzic and the other members of the leadership were investing efforts for the results of that meeting, either to be annulled or minimised, because the -- it gave the impression that something bad was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take that in stages, if we may. First of all, what did you understand was the purpose of forming this Bosnian Krajina community of municipalities, which subsequently became the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I have to say that I was not formally a member of that assembly. I think that the decision about it, at least according to my understanding, was influenced significantly by the war events in Croatia. It should be noted that this area borders on Croatia and that in Croatia at that time the conflict was already intensive between Croatia and the local Serbs in the area. In such an atmosphere, one needed to distinguish between what was happening in Banja Luka and Sarajevo. In Sarajevo this conflict was not even felt, but in Banja Luka, which was very close to those events, it was enveloped in an atmosphere which people felt, look in Croatia, there is the problem of Serbs, and we need to organise here too. And that is what could be intimated from the public reports. I really can't go into the thoughts of the people who formed those bodies. I said I wasn't a member. But I think that what was decisive for this was the war going on in Croatia at great intensity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may have been the motive but what was the purpose of the foundation of the -- first of all, the community of municipalities, which was formed before the war in Croatia broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It should be noted that even before the formation of that community, there was a regional association of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina. This association didn't have any prerogatives of power but it was rather designed to coordinate certain activities and develop joint projects so that region had been defined as such earlier on. Now, what could have been the reasons for forming the community of municipalities, I would say those were the coordination of activities to prevent any potential escalation of the war and its spreading from the territory of Croatia, and thereby to homogenise local communities so that the Serbs could be assisted who were engaged in conflict in Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this was -- you say -- to assist the Serbs in -- who were in the conflicts in Croatia itself. Was this organisation a Serbian organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It covered municipalities in which the Serbs constituted the majority as a rule. Of course there were representatives of other peoples. I don't think that the main intention was to provide any kind of military assistance. I know that humanitarian aid was being organised for Serbs in the area. At least to the best of my knowledge, because I said, as I said, I was far from the structures of government. So the main forms of assistance at the time was humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Were you in favour of the -- your municipality, Laktasi, joining this community?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: As you can see from this document, the municipal assembly did take a decision for the municipality to join. It should be noted that the SDS was in power in that municipality, they had absolute authority. We were in the Alliance of Reform Forces, the party I belonged to at the time, we believed that any move in that direction would further complicate the situation and our official position was that that was not necessary at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why did you believe that any move in that direction would further complicate the situation? What did you think was going to happen as a result of this community of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina at least one needs to view things in their entirety. Behind the political parties were movements designed to homogenise. Within the SDA, a Patriotic League had already been formed which had -- which rallied Muslims as a rule, which were preparing for an armed conflict or what they described as the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas on the other hand within the Serbian national Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. body or core, so-called autonomous regions were being formed in areas which were predominantly populated by Serbs. And that means Krajina, Semberija, Romanija, Herzegovina. Our position was that no political territorial organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be formed unilaterally but that they should be the result of political negotiation and agreement and that only after that should Bosnia-Herzegovina be finally constituted on the basis of agreement. So that we felt that any unilateral actions by various parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina further complicated things and moved us away from favourable results. On the other hand, the HDZ extended full support to the government in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment, sir, you may be asked questions about that but I'm just interested in why you didn't think it was a good idea for the Serbs to -- or Laktasi to join the community of municipalities. What did you think was the problem?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think I've already said, not just Laktasi, the formation of such an entity was an act that further complicated the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than contributing to a settlement. That was my general position, and it didn't apply only to Laktasi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you look, please, then, at an interview that you gave about this in April of 1991, published in Glas?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again this is a new exhibit. Which will become 2457.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving this press conference after the Laktasi municipality decided to join this community of associations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I remember that press conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you give your reasons for why you did not approve of the decision which had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, as is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can we just continue this topic, please, of regionalisation? Were you present at the second session of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina held in Sarajevo on the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was present. That assembly was operating but also the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So were you attending both assemblies then at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have for a moment the minutes of that session, which is P17. Was it at this session that the results of the plebiscite of the Serbian people, which had been held, was announced?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, as can be seen from the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want you to have a look, please, at the speech or part of the speech made by Mr. Krajisnik as president of the assembly. I'm not sure where you're going to find this in the B/C/S but our page 10 of the English translation, where he said, "We have a duty to determine the function of regions and autonomous districts with view to preserving the unity of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why we should not allow regions to become independent entities separate from the rest of the Serbian people. It is essential that the Serbian people organise themselves into one legal and state entity. One common state with all the other peoples who want to build a happier future with us." And so on. Did you understand that this was SDS policy that all Serbs were to live in one state, before even this speech of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I have to say that before that plebiscite of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were plebiscites of the Muslim and/or Bosniak and Croatian people several months before that and the atmosphere was gaining in intensity and I knew that at the time the leadership of SDS was not against Bosnia-Herzegovina but was for an agreement in which Bosnia and Herzegovina would fully protect national communities, and I know that the proposal was to introduce a chamber of peoples in the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that at the time, the dominant idea was that everything was being done, at least that was my understanding, should remain within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but with the right and possibility to protect in this case the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that very same time and even months before this and months after this, there was visible homogenisation along the same principles of both the Muslim and Croatian peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I can confirm that I did attend this assembly and I do remember this speech by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was this speech by Mr. Krajisnik a surprise to you, in other words that he was saying that the -- it was essential that the Serbian people organise themselves into one legal and state entity? Or was that something that you realised the SDS wanted to happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I must say that this did not come as much of a surprise, because practically everybody spoke the same way and in the same terms. In those days and months, this is absolutely the language that was being used. I could hear this coming from other quarters as well. So I have to confirm what I was confident of then and am today, that the leading party of the Serb people, the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina, believed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it should be preserved and that the Serb people should enjoy equal rights within Bosnia-Herzegovina and that Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain within Yugoslavia. That is how I understood the policy of that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you understood the words all Serbs should live in one legal and state entity to mean that it should enjoy equal rights within Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's what you're telling us, is it, Mr. Dodik? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it can be interpreted that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the way you interpreted it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can repeat what I said, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to know whether you interpreted it in that way? It's a simple yes or no, please. Otherwise you'll be here for much longer. Is that the way you interpreted it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was not my understanding that a particular people, ethnic group, could have exclusive rights in one territory but I did think that collective efforts had to be made in order to seek a peaceful solution to the problems of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'll ask you one more time because it's not an answer to my question. Did you understand Mr. Krajisnik, when he uttered those words, to be saying that this was a Serb state remaining within Bosnia and Herzegovina? Or did you understand it to mean that they -- the SDS were looking to set up a separate state?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. A certain collectivity within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll leave that. Now, did you also hear, and this is at our page 29 of the assembly, the translation of the meeting, the decision on the verification of the proclaimed Serbian autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where they verified the Autonomous Region of Krajina, made up of municipalities that they listed there, and then the other autonomous regions? Now, what did you understand was the purpose of setting up Serbian autonomous regions within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember what I thought at that point in time but at any rate the impression was that bearing in mind all round events and developments, that this was a normal thing, at least that's the way it was presented at the time, that within the territory where the Serbs were majority population, some autonomous regions should be organised that would have the task to coordinate activities. In the field of defence and in the field of coordinating overall life in those territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was this something, as you understood it from your knowledge and your discussions with people at the assembly, something that was part of a plan or something that was purely spontaneous?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I think that first forms of such organisation were spontaneous and then as you can see through this decision that was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. verified by the assembly, this indeed did assume an official nature and it was verified in such a way, these regions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we move, then, please, to the SDS itself as a party? Accepting that you weren't a member of the party, did you become familiar with the hierarchy of the party and the people who were in positions within that party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. This was generally known, who had which role within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, within the party hierarchy, was the leadership -- Dr. Karadzic as president of the party, at the top levels of the party, through its main board? Was the party controlled from the top?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Mr. Karadzic was president of that party, which had its main board.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if the main board issued instructions, were the municipal boards and the regional boards obliged to carry out those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That was quite clear. This was a firmly organised political party with clear-cut hierarchy and superior -- superiority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if the main board issued instructions to the regional board, were the regional board obliged to carry out those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this happened as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the regional board - I'll come on to the later organisations in a moment - issued instructions to the municipal boards, were those instructions binding on the municipal boards?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- sorry, Mr. Dodik, I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the way it was. The regional boards had a coordinating role, and I think that policies were agreed at that level, and this constituted a type of obligation and task for the lower levels in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we've spoken about the community of municipalities and then the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the assembly. You were not a member of that assembly, I think you've already told us. What sort of authority did that regional assembly have in respect of the municipal assemblies of the various municipalities that made up the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The assembly and the executive organ that was formed later, regulated all of life, political, economic, cultural, all segments of life. Decisions were passed and these decisions were observed by the municipalities that were members of these regional communities. It should be said that at that time it was quite obvious that there was total disorganisation in terms of the functioning of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and even some decisions related to the fiscal system were passed at the level of these regional communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How strong was the control and discipline that was exercised by the SDS over these bodies where they were the controlling party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that this party was internally highly homogenised and it functioned in a highly disciplined fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you've been asked if you could talk a little louder. I think if we can pull the microphone a little closer, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to members of the SDS who didn't agree with some of the decisions that were being made?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I think that they were minimised then, and that they turned passive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If someone made those -- his disagreement public by giving an interview or something like that, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It's important to refer to the exact period that is meant because even days counted in this respect. In 1991, until, say, April, 1992, absolutely people could express different views regarding certain matters, and as you could see, different political parties had their press conferences. After the conflict broke out in April in Bosnia-Herzegovina, divergent views did not merit media attention. The media only espoused official views. If somebody would come out with a position that was different from that of the ruling SDS then very often -- very easily they could be proclaimed a traitor. I'm talking about the time when the conflict had already broken out, so they could either be proclaimed traitors or somebody who was anational, unnational.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we just for a moment -- and I won't ask you to look at it, sir, but Mr. Krajisnik in the same assembly speech that he was making, said this: "On our way --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is page 12, Your Honours, of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "On our way to achieving the goals of the Serbian people, we accept all friends, we accept everybody except traitors and opponents. Traitors and outcasts are the most difficult opponents. We would like to send the following message to all those who falter or are neutral, weak, or misguided and who do not feel like traitors. Today you still have time. Tomorrow will be too late." In your view, from your knowledge, was that a sentiment that was typical of the way the SDS dealt with what they considered traitors or outcasts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Krajisnik was a highly placed member of the SDS and he was president of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and president of the parliament of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His public speeches, as a rule, were interpreted as the official stands of the party he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, you can take that document back. And I want to move now, please, to the events in 1992. And if we could have a look, please, at an article published or an interview published with Krajisnik and Brdjanin at the time of the Lisbon talks. It's Exhibit P117. Now, this was an interview apparently with Krajisnik as president of the Serbian an assembly and Brdjanin, then the vice-president of the assembly of the autonomous region and if you go to the question, "Are there differences between the republican and the Krajina SDS leaderships relative to that agreement?" Which is on the second page of the translation, and Brdjanin gave a reply in which he said: "For the people of Krajina, there exists but one option. The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina should grow out of two cantons, the first comprising the Krajina, Northern Bosnia, and Semberija, and the second Eastern Herzegovina and so on. We stand behind the SDS and the ministerial council of the Serbian assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but Sarajevo cannot be the centre of that republic, only Serbian Banja Luka." I want to deal later with what you know about Brdjanin and the other people. But at this stage, were you aware of ideas expressed by Brdjanin and others that the centre of what was the proposed Serbian republic should be in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't remember this interview, because already then it was difficult to obtain such newspapers that followed developments but from the very outset, when this political, territorial organisation was established of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a clash so to speak between -- regarding the centre, where it should be. Karadzic and his people thought that it should be Pale, and people from Krajina thought that Banja Luka should be the centre. Banja Luka was the biggest city and it had the infrastructure required for such an exercise. When I became Prime Minister, I transferred the seat of government from Pale to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He goes on to say a little later - and it's your knowledge I'm concerned about, not whether you read this article at the time - that the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina had voted, all had voted against the agreement and that if the Serbian assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not accommodate our requests by then, we shall proclaim the Serbian Republic of Krajina. And then it goes on and Krajisnik joins in. And again, he states that, in the next paragraph, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that there are certain groups who do not belong to the SDS who are holding even positions contrary to global SDS policy and the interests of the Bosnian Krajina, not under control of the SDS. While their activity cannot be underrated, it cannot be called traitorous. At that stage, as you have told us, or there was a struggle between Karadzic and the people in Krajina as to where the centre should be. In the end, as we know, the centre was in Pale. If Krajisnik and Brdjanin had held out for the centre to be in Banja Luka, from what you know of the SDS, would they have remained in the positions that they later held?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I think, I assume, no, because the top leadership of SDS, headed by Karadzic, was at that time the uncontested leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we then move, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to do, I know it's a little early but I'm going to do a series of events in Banja Luka as a group so it may be appropriate to take the break at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Korner, we will have a break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move, please, to the events in 1992. In 1992, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were still a deputy at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I was a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that unusual for someone in your position to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: There were certain decisions that deputies have their own mobilisation assignment within the parliament, so at least that was my understanding. It was unusual for members of parliament to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was a reserve officer of the former Yugoslav People's Army and the local authorities consisting of representatives of the SDS in my place of residence mobilised me, in my understanding, because I wasn't a member of their structure, their group, their party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that something that the SDS could use as a lever? In other words, that if someone didn't agree with their policies, or presented a problem to them, they could be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: There was a general mobilisation by then, and people who had a public role were perhaps mobilised for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal with what happened during the time you were mobilised. Were you at Laktasi airport, as part of your tasks when mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the Banja Luka airport in Laktasi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, you're quite right. And into what sort of unit had you been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I was in a police unit, which had duties with respect to the security of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember, at the beginning of April of 1992, the arrival of a group that went by the name of the SOS, the Serbian Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. They arrived at the airport and there was an air corridor provided from the Banja Luka airport for the transportation of men to Belgrade. They were there for one day, maybe a little longer, and they took over control of that transportation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people who were trying to leave, to go to Belgrade, what nationality were they, in the main?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: There were members of all nationalities. It should be noted that there was no land connection with Belgrade or that is Serbia, or with Croatia for that matter, and that the only way was to go by air. Quite a number of people fearing events that they saw as being tragic used this possibility to go towards Belgrade, and then from there possibly to Europe. There were Serbs, Croats and Muslims, but in the main, they were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, when the SOS arrived at the airport, what instructions were you given as to how you should treat the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Members of the military police unit, which I was a member, were withdrawn to the barracks and the actual area used for the control and movement of these people while boarding planes to go to Belgrade, this area was under the control of those SOS forces but this didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you understood it, was this SOS force approved by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They arrived unannounced, at least as far as I was concerned. It was a surprise for me. I do know that the airport command probably with their leaders had discussions and after a couple of hours, things were brought back to normal, at least that is the very next day. I hadn't had any information up until then of the existence of such forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but if a -- first of all I should ask you: Were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they in uniform of some kind?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The men at the airport were wearing uniforms, with hats on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you remember what colour the hats were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The same colour as their uniform, camouflage, military camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. These men were not part of the JNA, were they? They weren't regular army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That is how I saw them, but I really don't know whether formally they were or not but it was my impression that they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they members of the police? Military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can't confirm that because I really don't know, but I think, at least during their stay at the airport, they appeared to be acting independently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if an armed group of men arrived at the airport, would you expect that you would receive orders that they were to be prevented from taking over the airport?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that would be a normal order to expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you ever given any such order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at some articles or one in particular, I think will be sufficient, that deals with the SOS arrival in Banja Luka. That is, please, Exhibit P137. Now, I know you've had a chance to look at this before. Do you know whether or not you saw it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The demands that were being made by the SOS, in particular that people should be dismissed who were not, as it was put, I think, loyal to the Serbian republic and that a Crisis Staff should be set up, when you heard about this, did you form any view as to whether or not these people had any connection with the SDS in Banja Luka, or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It is rather hard for me to remember the thoughts I had at the time, but in any event, it seemed to me to be something that was resolved quickly, the situation caused by these forces was quickly addressed by official authorities. Now, whether this was in direct agreement with the SDS, I can only make assumptions about that. The situation was highly fluid, volatile, already, so I can only make an assumption and say that it is possible that there was some sort of coordination but I really can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want you to make assumptions, please, sir. Let's look at your own experience from when you were in government and as a member of the assembly originally. If an armed group had arrived in Banja Luka and demanded, first of all, that the lawful government should set up a Crisis Staff, is that something in your experience that you would have agreed to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course I wouldn't have been in the government at that time. Again, I can only make an assumption. I think that the appearance of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. men under arms in any town is a traumatic event and everything depended on their demands. I would consider whether I wanted to talk to them at all, whether I wanted to accept it or not, but I can only say once again that I do remember that those demands that same day that they were made, were in a sense accepted and acknowledged by those in power at the time in the municipal assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know that, sir. And that's what I'm asking you. I appreciate you weren't in power at the time but I'm asking you whether, in your experience, without further ado, if an armed band of men came into town and made a series of demands, which affected government, would you have accepted those demands should be met without any attempt to get rid of this particular group?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to that. That question calls for pure speculation. Guessing, to make assumptions, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Objection overruled, Mr. Ackerman. It's a very relevant question. Please proceed, Ms. Korner. And, Witness, please answer the question. It's being put to you that you are fully aware of what the political situation was then. All you're being asked to consider is had you been in the place where the government was at the time, or other members were in government at the time, how would you have acted? It's not speculation. It's looking back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can say the following: I could have been in power then but I didn't want to be because of that situation. And probably hypothetically let me say, if I had been in organs of government, I certainly wouldn't have lightly accepted any groups to appear outside the system of armed forces and I would have taken certain steps. So it is a hypothetical question and a hypothetical answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Dealing with the hypothetical, what steps would you have taken?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I would have engaged the lawful police units and prevented the movement of those forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, that was the first establishment of a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka; do you agree with that? Or official establishment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The period after that was one when the Crisis Staff was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the people who was put on to this Crisis Staff was a man named Nenad Stevandic. And in the article I think he is quoted, yes, if we look under SOS demands accepted in the translation, which is on the third page, and then go over to page 4, "the Crisis Staff concluded that the Presidency of the Socialist Serbian Republic," I think probably, not sure which, "should be informed of these demands by Nenad Stevandic, the head of the Serbian Sokol society for the Krajina district." Did you know Stevandic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I heard of him. I didn't know him at the time. I met him later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether or not he had any connection with this group of people calling themselves the SOS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can't be precise about it but I think he was within that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment. Your Honour, the -- unless it's a bad translation, the exhibit that I'm looking at says that: "the Crisis Staff concluded that the presidency of the SFRY should be informed," and that's not what appears in the transcript. It's -- the transcript says something like Socialist Serbian Republic and SFRY is Yugoslavia the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So I don't know what the confusion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The two are different definitely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For a moment I hesitate because I wasn't sure whether it was meant to be that or the Serbian republic, but that's right. I agree with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So point taken, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you. That's all I want to ask you about the SOS. I want to move, then, please, to the 12th of May assembly. Did you attend that assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you have, please, Exhibit P50? I want to ask you a couple of questions about things that were said there. I'd like you to look, please, if you can find it in the speech of Mr. Krajisnik -- I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic, it's our page 13, where he set out the six strategic goals or he set out the strategic goals, which happened to be six. It's at page 13 of the translation. Do you remember him mentioning that these were the goals of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I do remember. I remember that this was discussed at the time, that those aims were presented for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: By Karadzic, I'm sorry, by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The first goal was: "separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century to attack us and who would continue with these practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." Listening to that, who did you understand Dr. Karadzic meant by the "enemies"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The enemy forces were already distinguishable. On the one side, there were groups linked to the Serb people, and on the other side were the Bosniak and Croat peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want then to move, please, to the speech that was made by Dragan Kalinic if you could find that. It's at our page 22 in the translation. Mr. Kalinic said in the second paragraph: "Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason. And I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious, they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people." First of all, was that the same Mr. Kalinic who had resigned with you from the Reformist Party?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same man, but if I may, I would comment on the first paragraph. Mr. Kalinic says that he's speaking on behalf of an independent group of deputies and I deny that, because it wasn't on behalf of an independent group of deputies because it hadn't been formed at the time. So he may have been speaking in his own name and in the name of a certain number of other people, but certainly not in my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that's what I was going to ask you. As you say, he said that he was speaking on behalf of the independents and you were one of them. Were these sentiments, Mr. Dodik, something that you had expected him to say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That point in time, I certainly didn't expect him to speak on behalf of this independent group of deputies, but I must say that it was a highly inspired speech, and it was quite well received by the other deputies in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, he was saying that he wanted the enemies physically and militarily destroyed and crushed and that of course meant eliminating and liquidating their key people. Were those sentiments that you expected him to express?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. He said that, not I, and I do remember that moment. I didn't expect such an approach.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we then -- I'm sorry, final question on that. What happened to Mr. Kalinic politically, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He shortly after that became a member of government or maybe he already was a member, as Minister of Health. After the war, he became president of the SDS and today he's president of parliament of Republika Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srpska and president of that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we then move on, please, in there to the speech made by Mr. Brdjanin, and this is page 29 of our translation, if you can find it in the original, Mr. Brdjanin, right at the beginning of his speech, effectively says this: "I would like to say a heartfelt bravo to Mr. Kalinic. In all my appearances in this joint assembly, it has never crossed my mind that although he seems quiet, while I seem hawkish, his opinions are the closest to mine." Can we move, please, to your knowledge of Mr. Brdjanin? When did you first get to know him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: When we were elected together to the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina as Members of Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In, first of all, his public speeches, how did his views strike you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He took part in parliamentary debates often. I've already said that at first there were three parties that formed the government, the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, and the MPs always spoke in defence of that government. Later on, various things happened and only political issues were dealt with by the assembly. A large number of people took part in this, including Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. What were his speeches like? Were they quiet, restrained, conservative? Were they extreme, noisy, aggressive? How would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the atmosphere in the assembly. If the assembly atmosphere was tolerant, then the speech would be quiet, and if it was heated, then practically everybody, including Mr. Brdjanin, introduced a certain dose of rhetoric, very pronounced rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you able to gauge from his public attitude, from what he said in public, what his view of non-Serbs remaining in a Serbian state was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Again, I have to set the exact time frame. These three nationalist parties, the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, formed joint local government in Banja Luka. I know that the HDZ gave the vice-president of the government in Banja Luka. So at that time, there was a dose of tolerance that was portrayed to the public on the part of these structures. However, when the conflict broke out and when the problems became obvious, then people from the SDS promoted the policy of resolving problems in a way which can be seen from these documents. But I also have to say that at that time, the media included the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and when somebody spoke in Banja Luka on one day it was impossible to distinguish it from what was said in Sarajevo and elsewhere, because at that time all speeches were rather emotional and they were aimed at mobilisation and homogenisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You drifted rather from the actual question I asked, which was what were Mr. Brdjanin's attitudes, and let's take it in 1991, first of all, to non-Serbs remaining in a Serbian state, between October and December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, in such terms of time, but I think that then there was not a policy of full intolerance yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: In 1991, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When, in your view, did the policy of full intolerance as you've described it, come into effect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: After -- I mean I've already said that June of 1991 is an important point in time, when Mr. Izetbegovic spoke of the right of Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia and that is when the parties that were in power started diverging significantly. However, the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually broke up in January or perhaps in the beginning of February, 1992. I think that after that, there weren't any sessions of parliament any more, at least not with all the MPs present. I was not present either. And after -- after the 6th of April, in essence there was a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So due to everything that was going on at the time, there was increasing national ethnic intolerance coming from all quarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We are dealing with Banja Luka, please. When do you say in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, it's impossible to talk about Banja Luka if you don't bear in mind the overall context of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether that in your view that's right or wrong, I am just asking you about Banja Luka. When did the policy of full intolerance, as you have described it, come into effect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It reflected the overall atmosphere and I've already said, after the well known decision made on the 6th of April, when certain structures of the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, the political representatives of an entire people did not agree to that. I have to be very specific; this term, "full intolerance," is something that perhaps never came to life in Banja Luka. There were certain things that happened but it is a well-known fact that in Banja Luka, practically all the time there were Bosniaks and Croats, a number of them, who went on living there throughout. However, problems were considerably on the rise after the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Regionalisation as a concept, we know was discussed in various meetings of the assemblies up until 1992. Did you find out what Mr. Brdjanin's view was in respect of regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brdjanin was an active participant in this process, and I think that later he was one of the more important people amongst the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at what stage was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, I can't place it exactly, this particular event of establishing the leadership, but from the very outset, when regional organs of government were established in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look, please, next, at a list of the regional Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, which is Exhibit P168. This is the decision dated the 5th of May, so a week or so before the assembly meeting, appointing the -- what's described as the war staff of the autonomous region with Radoslav Brdjanin as president and then vice-president Lieutenant Colonel Sajic and various other people. Now, Kupresanin was a mere member of the Crisis Staff, the regional Crisis Staff, but had been, had he not, the president of the regional assembly? Is that right? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you know Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We know from other evidence that the formation of these Crisis Staffs from the assemblies should have had the president of the assembly as president of the Crisis Staff. Do you know why Brdjanin became president instead of Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You knew both men. Is there anything in the character of either or both men that provides, in your view, an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They were prominent people at that point in time. I really cannot assess why this happened, why Mr. Brdjanin was president rather than Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us that the regional assembly, because of the hierarchies established within the SDS, had power over the municipal assemblies. Did the regional Crisis Staff, when it was set up, have the same powers as the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As president of the Crisis Staff, did Brdjanin have power?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I really am not aware of formal powers, but I believe that as president, he had the right to run that Crisis Staff and that he represented it in public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the function of the president that he, however decisions were taken within the Crisis Staff, that he had to sign decisions before they could be enacted? Was that an important function?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that the basic duty of the president is to sign the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents of the organ that he or she heads, that is to say decisions that are adopted at sessions of that body.
