utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you knew also, I think, well, perhaps, looking at the list, did you know all of these people or were there any that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I knew a considerable majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if you can just tell us who you didn't know. I think you told us that you met Stevandic later.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about him but I didn't know him at the time. I met him only after the war. At that time, I did not know of Slobodan Dubocanin. I did not know Zoran Jokic, I didn't know who he was either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to deal with first of all Vukic. At that stage, what sort of influence did he have as far as the Banja Luka authorities were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Dr. Radislav Vukic was president or a member of the municipal board of the SDS in Banja Luka, I think, and therefore he had an important position amongst the authorities as well, in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Predrag Radic, what about him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: He was president of the municipal assembly of Banja Luka, and that is the strongest and most powerful municipality in that region. I think that he was also a member of the SDS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the terms of the relationship between him and Brdjanin and Vukic, Vukic as head of the regional SDS board, Brdjanin as president of the regional Crisis Staff, and Predrag Radic as president of the municipality of Banja Luka, how did -- how would those three interact, together, as far as decision-making was concerned, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It is obvious that I was not a member of this organ, but I can tell you of my impressions at the time. Mr. Brdjanin appeared in public, but as far as true power of decision-making within this organ is concerned, that is what other people had. That's the impression I had as well as others. I think that Mr. Vukic and others had much more influence over the process of decision-making. I think that Mr. Radic himself, as president of the largest municipality, also had a significant role in the work of that particular organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Brdjanin being the public face of the Crisis Staff, Vukic and others having more influence in the process of decision-making, why did you get that impression?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I've already said that it's an impression. That's as far as I knew the situation and relationships there and that's what I inferred on the basis of many conversations with people who then and later confirmed such impressions. Mr. Vukic was president of the SDS and I think that he had formal power and also actual power in terms of effecting decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the reason being what, because of his position within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think so, yes. So as far as the authorities in Banja Luka during this period, May of 1992 until around September, the decision-making was that being made by the SDS? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, the SDS was the party in power, and at that time it certainly conceived of the policy that was pursued at the time by the organs that functioned as state organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again, from how you gained the impression, talking to people and the like, why was Brdjanin the public face of this organisation, if Vukic and Radic actually had more power?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin himself with greater power too at the time. He commanded the police. It seemed to me that this was some kind of a coordination staff that coordinated the work of various authorities, the police, the various municipal authorities, the military. I really cannot confirm the reasons, I mean why Mr. Brdjanin was president of this staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As far as Mr. Brdjanin's speeches or public utterances, whether reported on television or in the media, went, were his views -- were his views, in your view, conservative views, extreme views, tolerant views, what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They were clear, concise. At that time, they were geared towards concrete events and concrete things that were happening, and they did not really leave any scope for further dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want then, please, finally, to deal with two topics. The camps that were set up in various municipalities that came within the autonomous region, Omarska and the like. Did you hear about those camps at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you became aware that these camps existed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I've already said that I was in a police unit at the airport in Banja Luka. I cannot say which date and when, but I know that Mr. Kouchner came to visit the region at the time and he was a representative of the WHO or some other international organisation at the time. When he came to the airport then - I was there in the same room - he said that he came to see for himself whether certain talk in the western media about the existence of camps was true or not. That's the first time I heard of the possibility of them being in existence at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you discover the type of regime that had been operating in these camps, in particular in Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you heard about what had been happening in them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if the regional Crisis Staff, as the regional body of authority, with authority over the municipal Crisis Staffs, had wanted to prevent the camps being set up, could they have done so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that, because here in this Crisis Staff I don't see anyone who was from Prijedor, and I don't know what the relationships were like between the staff in Prijedor and this regional staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's mention Manjaca instead of Omarska and Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Manjaca, you knew about Manjaca, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the media as well. I think it was treated as a collection centre at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question again, because if you recall, Mr. Dodik, you were asked this when you were interviewed. In your view, knowing what you know from your political life, of the authority of the regional Crisis Staff, could they have prevented or indeed if they had wanted to, shut down those camps? Did they have that authority?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Formally speaking, yes. In essence, everything was based on strong local individuals, because I know in Prijedor, it was Simo Drljaca who was such a strong individual. And I cannot confirm that this staff could have exercised any significant influence over him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which staff, the Prijedor or the regional?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The regional one, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. So when you told us earlier that the regional Crisis Staff had the authority to prevent the camps, that you now think was a mistake, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't know if that's exactly the way I had put it, but at any rate I said that formally the regional organs had authority over the lower-level organs. From the point of view of such an interpretation, it is logical that they could have affected the decisions of the local communities. But what I wish to say is the fact that in many municipalities, there were strong, local persons who at given points in time, and in certain activities, had full independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, which municipalities had strong local persons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Prijedor did, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who in Prijedor? You've mentioned Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think he was chief of police. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. I met him later, after the war. At that time, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so you're basing your assessment of him as a strong local personality on what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I'm basing it on conversations with people who were familiar with the situation, with whom I had contacts later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then you said that these persons at given points in time and in certain activities had full independence. First of all, what point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I meant certain activities, what was going on within local clashes, in Prijedor, from what I know. I know that it was only local people who were of key importance, and in other places, too. I cannot give an assessment but I don't know. Perhaps there was coordination between the Crisis Staffs, but I'm not aware of this coordination. Perhaps this did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you've described not so long ago the regional Crisis Staff as a coordinating body.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that there was no one from Prijedor on that staff, at least I can't see anyone here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if you look down at -- on the main staff, no, but if you look down at number 16 on this item, does it say, "presidents of municipalities"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think presidents of municipalities were included, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally, I just want to ask you about the media generally. You've touched on this subject before. Once the conflict broke out in April 1992, in your view, how did the media behave? Were they reporting independently or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That depended on which part of Bosnia-Herzegovina they were based. The media sided with the local or regional authorities. And I think that from then on, they became propaganda instruments of the authorities everywhere, both of those in Sarajevo and in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Already earlier on, a number of people who were not suited in the view of the authorities were replaced by party men. The same applied to the SDA, the HDZ and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As far as the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was concerned, did Velibor Ostojic become the Minister of information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was control exercised over the media, and if so how?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: By the Ministry of the Government. There were regular briefings, and the control was up to the level of censorship so only what was suited to the authorities was published. And I really do think that this applied to all the sides equally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Ackerman is going to cross-examine you, sir, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's now good afternoon, Mr. Dodik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you just some very, very brief questions, and move rather rapidly because Ms. Korner covered this mostly, about your political career. This alliance of reformist forces that you were involved in, when that party was formed, did you play a role, any role, in the formation of that party or was it a party that you just joined or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I played an important role. The party was formed at a well-known rally attended by about 100.000 people on Mount Kozara at Mrakovica and it was addressed by the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, after which the initiative was launched to set up the party. And I was president of the regional organisation of that party from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case, isn't it, that part of the platform of that party was the preservation of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I said that earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. When the nationalist parties started being formed in anticipation of the multi-party elections, what was the first of the nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: The first to be formed was the national party of the Bosniak people, the SDA. The HDZ had already been formed in Croatia before that, and after the SDA, the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed, and a few months prior to the elections, the SDS was formed. So it was the last in the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the SDA was formed, was it not under the leadership of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Alija Izetbegovic was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was a well-known person in Yugoslavia at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Increasingly well-known. Up until then he was known exclusively as a member of a group that promoted the ideas of Muslim fundamentalism and he was known to have spent time in prison in Foca as a result of those activities, and he also wrote a book along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did that history of his, when he then became head of the SDA, the basically Muslim nationalist party, that history of his, I take it, was well known and played some role in the way other people reacted to the formation of that party. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think you're quite right. His role was well-known, and the judgements against him were public so that many people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were aware of his engagements, and I could agree with you that this served for many as motives for their subsequent behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So to some extent, would you say that the creation of the SDS was very much a reaction to the way the SDA was created and under whose leadership it was created?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was concern, was there not, when the issue came about regarding what was going to happen with Bosnia-Herzegovina and where it would be within Yugoslavia, if within Yugoslavia at all, there was concern, was there not, about the motivation of Mr. Izetbegovic in his efforts to create an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all politicians in Bosnia and Herzegovina were convinced that Izetbegovic wanted an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and that his public speeches had -- were only part of a strategy to obtain that goal, even though they may have sounded as if they advocated measures to preserve Yugoslavia. So the impression was of most people, including myself, that Izetbegovic wanted an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the same sort of shape in which it had existed up until then, of course, but renouncing its socialist character.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a number of people also believed, based upon the prior history of Mr. Izetbegovic, that his goal was to create an Islamic state in Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: A number of people, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber, and I think you probably know this quite well, tell the Chamber why it was that the Serbs felt so strongly about the need to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Most Serbs in those days considered it to be quite normal that they should be in the community of Serbia as the motherland and that the form of order for Bosnia-Herzegovina should be such that it should remain in a community, in an agreed community, with Serbia and the other republics wishing to remain within Yugoslavia. The main thesis, the main goal, was to remain in Yugoslavia. Later on, if Slovenia and the other republics left, the other republics that didn't want to remain in Yugoslavia, this thesis was called in question. On the other hand, there was widespread conviction among the Serbs that Mr. Tudjman's regime was identical to the one that existed in the period from 1941 to 1945, and that for those reasons, Serbs could not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. feel safe in Croatia and therefore not in Krajina either. Because there were certain aspirations by the Tudjman regime towards that Krajina - when I say Krajina, I mean the Banja Luka Krajina - and this was later confirmed by various witnesses like Mr. Ashdown, who spoke a map drawn by Tudjman from which it could be seen that the Banja Luka region, according to this division advocated by Tudjman, should have been annexed to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the transcript, 54, line 22 I think the witness said most Serbs in those days considered it to be quite normal that they should be in a community with Serbia, not of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- sir, let me read out to you what we have in the English transcript of what you're supposed to have said. And then having heard what Mr. Ackerman has just stated, tell me whether you want to enter any correction. You were asked: "Tell the Chamber, and I think you probably flow this quite well, tell the Chamber why, why it was that the Serbs felt so strongly about the need to keep Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia?" And your answer was as follows: "Most Serbs in those days considered it to be quite normal that they should be in the community of Serbia as the motherland." It is being suggested that you didn't say "in the community of Serbia as the motherland," but you stated in the community with Serbia as the motherland. Is what is being suggested by Mr. Ackerman correct? Or is what we have in the transcript, which reflects correctly what you stated earlier on in your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People felt that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be in a community with Serbia, and virtually 100 per cent of the Serbs in Bosnia considered Serbia to be the motherland. They were never in favour of abolishing Bosnia-Herzegovina or separating it. The idea was to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course in a redefined form, and as such, in a community with other republics wishing to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now for a few moments about the referendum on independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was a subject that began being discussed in parliament as the year of 1991 was coming to an end, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have said, and I'm quoting, "We in the opposition considered this to be a very serious matter which could provoke a major crisis and even war. We felt that this issue should have been avoided." That was in your testimony in Plavsic, page 471, line 20. First of all, let me ask you how you believe that it could have been avoided, in your view? How could the issue have been avoided, about independence, the referendum?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Let me confirm this statement as mine. I think it was clear, and we realised that in the opposition, that a decision on the referendum was being taken only by representatives of the Bosniak and Croatian people, that representatives of the Serbian people were excluded from taking that decision in the assembly, and it was quite normal that representatives of the SDA and HDZ had a majority in parliament at the time so from the formal standpoint, it was possible for them to take such a decision but it was quite clear that the procedure of outvoting was underway, outvoting everyone nation so we in the opposition felt that a solution should be found through negotiation and not through outvoting. I must say that I didn't take part in that referendum. I know it was held in the spring of 1992. And facts show that almost as a rule, or the absolute majority of the Serbs did not take part in that referendum. So our opinion in the opposition at the time was that every move, including this one, regarding a referendum that had unilateral political meaning, should be halted until a final agreement was reached by all relevant political forces so that an agreed restructuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina could take place. These were visible efforts by all groupings on all sides to implement the policy that they were advocating at the time. Izetbegovic himself, expounding on the need to do this, said in parliament, I remember this sentence of his, that he was ready to sacrifice peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the subject of subsequent considerable political debate and confrontations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You indicated that, "it was our opinion in the opposition, that these moves should be halted until a final agreement was reached by all relevant political forces so that agreed restructuring could take place," leaving out some of your words. Was that an opinion that you voiced in the parliament? Was it something that you and other people were arguing at the time in the parliament, let's back off, let's not go there, let's see if we can come to some kind of an agreement? Were you making those kinds of arguments?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. A certain number of people felt that way. Later on, the referendum was the cause for my leaving the party, the Alliance of Reformist Forces, because representatives of that party, my former colleagues, were in favour of having the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back now to your statement in the Plavsic case again and just read it again, "We in the opposition considered this to be a very serious matter which could provoke a major crisis and even war." My question to you now, at the time, in the parliament, did all of -- did the parties in the parliament who were struggling with this issue understand it in that way? That it was a serious matter which could provoke a major crisis and even war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can't confirm that with respect to other political parties but my feeling was that people were determined to carry out their plans regardless of the horrors of war that this could provoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us this? And I'd ask you in trying to give us your answer to this, that you not use the value of hindsight but try to think of what you saw at the time and what you felt at the time, what you knew at the time. What was it that the Serbs believed would happen if Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent rather than remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Serbia? Or Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me rephrase that again just to make sure we get it right. What I want you to try to tell us, if you can, trying to dredge up your memory of that moment, those moments in parliament, and not with the value of hindsight, what was it the Serbs believed would happen if Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent rather than remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: They had experience with respect to the decision on the referendum in the assembly where they had been outvoted and they felt that this system of outvoting would predominate and that decisions which would affect significantly the lives of all in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be taken through a coalition of two peoples against the third, and that was what the people felt, what they feared, that developments would have -- lead to institutions as it had up until then, in which peoples would be outvoted. I know that an effort was made to set up a chamber of peoples as a second chamber of the assembly but that was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you talk about outvoting, you refer, of course, to the vote that was taken in the parliament regarding the referendum was an outvoting in that one nation was excluded --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talk about the fear being that in the future, in an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, that that would become the norm, and that minority rights would simply not be recognised any longer. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, only the Serbs were not then or now either a minority people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they are a constituent people. But in 1992, this constituent character of theirs was not recognised through this voting in parliament, and this instilled fresh fear in people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now I will let you use some hindsight. Looking back from the perspective you have today, do you believe that those fears that you've expressed, that the Serbian people had in 1991, early 1992, were justified Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and realistic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And can you elaborate on that at all? And if you can, please do.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can say a couple of things. First, that historical experience that was dominant in the understanding of the political situation among the Serbs was very strong. The experience linked to the previous war, the Second World War, when Serbs in those areas suffered considerably at the hands of the independent state of Croatia. The experiences from that war also showed that Croats and Bosniaks, or rather Muslims in those days, were even then together in military units, which had as their aim or their target the Serbian people. And this fear was heightened by the lack of readiness by the partners in government, as they called themselves at the time, to acknowledge any demands so that the policies in Bosnia and Herzegovina in those days could be described as one of stubbornness, digging in of one side in relation to the other. People were terrified and only the truth that the dominant party in a certain people wanted to present them in, the SDA, to the Muslims, the SDS to the Serbs and the HDZ to the Croats. The Serbs had the greatest fear due to their experience from the Second World War, and also the refusal to introduce the Chamber of Peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina in those days, and to recompose Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course in 1991, the events you've discussed were fairly recent in time and there were a number of people alive who had experienced those events in the 1940s, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, at the end of the session, we need to decide the matter that you raised in private session this morning. Please do remind me in case --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I have a matter that I'd like to raise. It's quite brief, so I'll remind you if you'll remind me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll certainly remember. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dodik, I want to ask you now when it was that you first met Radoslav Brdjanin, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't remember the actual event, but I know that it was at one of the first sessions of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1990, immediately after the elections actually, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Had you heard of him before that or was that the first time that you had either heard of him or met him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Of course I heard of him. I knew that he worked in a construction company in Banja Luka, but I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had a conversation with Ms. Korner on 16 June of 2003, and Ms. Korner asked you then about Brdjanin, how well you knew him. And your answer was: "Not very well, we were in conflict." Can you tell me what you meant by your answer: "We were in conflict"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: We were in different political parties. That's the conflict I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were just speaking of the fact that were you in a different party from him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. And we had different political organisations and therefore we had different views regarding certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look again at Prosecutor's Exhibit 168, please. Now, this is the document you were looking at earlier today. It's a decision on the formation of the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and I have a few questions I want to ask you about that document. First of all, if you look at the very first paragraph, it indicates that the decision was made pursuant to Article 12 of the law on National Defence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what Article 12 of the law on National Defence is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing that I'd like to bring to your attention is that the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is created not by the assembly of ARK but by the executive council. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I see it. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would something like this be done by the executive council instead of by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Perhaps circumstances led to that. I really cannot guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there certainly wasn't, you know, heavy fighting going on in the Banja Luka municipality on the 5th of May, 1992, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That there was not, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, there was no fighting, there were no military operations, but the general atmosphere was that of a war. There was a war psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The document seems to be signed by a person by the name of Nikola Erceg. Did you know Nikola Erceg and do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Nikola Erceg was also a member of parliament, and that's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was the president of the executive council of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on 5 May, 1992, when he signed this decision. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I know that the was president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who else was on the executive council?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You notice that --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You notice that Mr. Erceg appointed himself as a member of the war staff. You see that? Number 4?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I see that. I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he also appointed Mr. Kupresanin the president of the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in assuming that Mr. Erceg had, and his executive council, had the power to create such a war staff or would that be wrong? Do you know whether they had the power to actually do this or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If I knew the essence of the law on National Defence, and Article 12, then perhaps I could answer the question. At that time, all the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Yugoslavia were in force in the area. I really don't know what Article 12 of this law pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it makes sense, if it's true, that Mr. Erceg did have the power to create this war staff, doesn't it also make sense that he would have the power to dissolve it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. Those who create something or establish it have such authority, and powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Brdjanin, you've talked about this earlier today, although Brdjanin appears there as president of the Crisis Staff, you've told us that in your view, he was not the most powerful person on that staff, that there were other people on there that were more powerful than he, including Predrag Radic and Radislav Vukic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. That's the impression that we had then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you said not only was it the impression that you had then but it's the impression that you got from talking to a lot of people afterwards also?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had an interview that was tape recorded in Banja Luka on 17 July, 2003. Do you remember that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: If that was recorded, then indeed it did take place. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They want you to speak a little louder.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. A few interviews with me were conducted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this one, you were being asked about the same issue that I'm talking to you about, Brdjanin's role in the Crisis Staff. You said on page 5, line 23 of the English version, "In other words, if Brdjanin wanted to implement anything with the Crisis Staff, he had to ask for the approval of Radic. Without that, he couldn't have done anything." Do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, that was my opinion. I was not present at these meetings but this is an opinion that corroborates the previously mentioned position, namely that Mr. Brdjanin was not the most influential member of that staff and quite simply that people were there who had far greater power and who were in such offices. I already mentioned the chief of police, the presidents of the municipality, the president of the SDS. So they had these positions, they held these offices, and they were on the staff ex officio and the implementation of these decisions depended on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, just so we can save a little bit of time, when you say to us that it is your impression or you have the opinion, that's based not only upon your observations at the time but on your conversations with people since that time, up until fairly recent times; am I correct in that? In other words, you're not just guessing. This is based upon something that you observed and have heard?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 7 in that same interview we were just talking about, you were talking about Dr. Vukic, and you were explaining how to be head of the regional board of the SDS, he would have had to have had a very direct link with Karadzic, and couldn't have done -- couldn't have gotten where he did without the complete support and approval of Karadzic, and you described him as, "He was the most important person in all of this." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that it can be put that way, that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What about a person named Jovan Cizmovic? What do you know about him? Anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I heard of him, but I know little about his activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think you probably were in some assembly sessions where there was a great deal of disagreement, dissension, going on between Karadzic on the one hand and Brdjanin on the other, primarily over the issue of where the government was going to be headquartered, in Pale or Banja Luka. Do you remember some of those sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I remember. I've already confirmed that, when I spoke to the Prosecutor. I think that this was a continuous theme. At every session, that issue was raised, within any item on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, that was a constant theme of Mr. Brdjanin's, right up until the time that Ms. Plavsic brought the government to Banja Luka [Realtime transcript read in error "mruuk"] and then you followed her lead in that regard, or you made your own decision in that regard, I suppose, but that was Brdjanin's contention throughout that whole period, that the seat of government belonged in Banja Luka, not in Pale, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And that tension that Brdjanin was part of, was a tension that stayed there right up until the time that Mrs. Plavsic actually moved the government to Banja Luka, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that this went on on a continuous basis until the government moved to Banja Luka. Others advocated it too but I remember that Mr. Brdjanin persisted the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Nenad Stevandic. Do you think he had more power than Mr. Brdjanin had?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot assess that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 67, line 3, has the word "mruuk," and it should be Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That goes down for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that was going to get fixed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you in Banja Luka very much during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: No. In 1992, I was mobilised, and I was within the police unit at the airport, which was about 25 or 30 kilometres away from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were there most of the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked by Ms. Korner about the visits of various internationals, heads of international groups, things like that, that came to Banja Luka and came to the area, and it seemed that they never met with Brdjanin but did meet with people like Radic and Kupresanin and Zupljanin and Vukic, persons like that. One of the things that I want to ask you about that is: Wasn't it the case during this time, and when I say "this time," I'm talking about late 1991, early 1992, that there were people who had titles and people who had power and they weren't necessarily the same people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think in -- when you were talking with Ms. Korner, I have some notes of that conversation, she asked you about this. Page 4 of those notes. She said to you the international community often met with Radic, not Brdjanin. Why? And it's recorded that you said this: "Brdjanin is crazy, he took our public face. Radic conducted the policies. That is why the international community went to where the power was, Radic.", true?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you read the next line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you can read it if you want to. I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: A considerable part of that is correct. Mr. Brdjanin had a hypothetical view. He took public responsibility for many things that were happening so that's why it can all be put under quotation marks. It is correct, this was a fact. However, the fact that everybody went to see Radic was a result of the fact that he was president of the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, as you sit here today, do you know anyone who, in early 1992, who was actually a subordinate of Brdjanin's, someone who had to do Brdjanin's bidding, who had to follow his orders, who had no choice with regard to Mr. Brdjanin but to do what he said? Do you know of anybody who was in that position, that he was actually the superior of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Directly, the way you've put it, I really cannot give a single name, but it is a fact that there was this Crisis Staff and then one can speak of subordination in terms of this hierarchy, and that's the way I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess if you would sit down and draw a chart where you would put the ARK Crisis Staff and then under that you'd put the municipalities, then it would appear by looking at that chart that the Crisis Staff had some power and authority regarding those municipalities, but I think you also know and you've told us today that a lot of those municipalities and particularly powerful individuals within them were operating rather independently. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, they were autonomous. They were the strong individuals in those local communities. I think that they had stronger links to the top echelons of government then, Karadzic at the time, rather than with the Crisis Staff and other regional organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If, for instance, Brdjanin had ordered someone to do something and Radic or Vukic or a gentleman named Vlado Kovacevic had said no, you don't have to do that, they wouldn't have done it, would they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the contrary, if Brdjanin ordered somebody not to do something who had been told by Radic, Vukic or Kovacevic to do something, they would likely go ahead and do it. That's also true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, following that logic, possibly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you talked with Mr. Tiger --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: May I just say something? In relation to these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: This is an unauthorised statement on my part. Many things here do not reflect what was said, and perhaps these are mistakes made by the interpreters. And therefore, I cannot say that this is a fact, especially as far as certain sections are concerned. This cannot be considered a proper document because I did not authorise it and I did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's absolutely fair. And I accept that. And I'll be a little bit more careful in the way I ask you questions about these documents with that in mind, okay? I do want to ask you about a paragraph that appears in a document that is called investigators's notes. These are notes made by an investigator of conversations you had with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should add it's a number of conversations. If you look at the front you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I said conversations, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, you said a conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's clear from -- these are interpreter's notes actually or investigator's notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are notes and they are not signed by him. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 19 and 20 I said exactly that. Made by an investigator of conversations you had with Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman, because we are approaching quarter to 2 very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just for a moment - I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Ackerman - go into private session just to mention one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while. Yes, Ms. Korner, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now we have just been talking about a group whose names I won't mention again, sir. Would you agree with the proposition that their influence on events around Banja Luka was decisive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that this group, or members of it, attempted to gain command over the army but didn't succeed completely in doing so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: Well, from the very beginning, it was quite clear that there were differences between military and civilian structures and the civilian authorities persistently endeavoured to impose its influence over the military, and there were various stages, such as in 1993, when that conflict between the military and civilian bodies escalated in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you describe that in a little more detail? There was a conflict actually between Karadzic and the military, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DODIK
utterances.text: It was a rather specific situation, and it depended on the period. Even on the day we are talking about, the situation was one in April and quite different already in May, as far as that is concerned. So the fact that the Yugoslav People's Army still existed and there was total confusion regarding civilian competence over that army, and there were conflicts between the civilian authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and the army. Later on, when the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, this problem was overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to a whole new subject now and I want to talk a little bit -- Ms. Korner talked to you a little bit about the media and I want to ask you a question or two about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I have another 30 to 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we better stop now with the witness and do the rest of the business that remains on our table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make a request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we finish our work today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's difficult and we have 45 minutes and we are allotted time only until quarter to 2.00 where we have to stop because the courtroom is taken over by another Trial Chamber so I'm afraid, I had hoped that we would finish with you today but things don't always go the way we desire. So we'll have to meet again tomorrow morning. I assume that within an hour or so you will be out of this courtroom tomorrow morning. I thank you, sir, for understanding and for being patient. The usher will escort you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman, I understand you needed to raise some further point before we handed down our decision. Do we stay in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is a completely different issue, Your Honour. We were just during one of the breaks we were talking about what the status of the Talic exhibits are and we just want to make sure that there is an order on the record by Your Honours that those exhibits become part of the new Brdjanin indictment because many of the exhibits that came in through Talic were exhibits that I would have put in had they not done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I raised it because it suddenly occurred to me what their status was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right both of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the sense that the trial was severed off and presumably the exhibits went with that part of the trial. Your Honour, I have no objection to that at all. I simply ask this: Whether we need to have all of them. In other words, I know Mr. Ackerman may want to use some of them but do we actually want all of them in the case. I mean, it's just mounting up the exhibits, that's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's probably a stack this high. There are very few, there 26, I think, in total. As I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion let's be practical about it. Let's admit them all or declare that they still form part of these proceedings, for all intents and purposes, and that they should be preserved in the records of these proceedings and that effectively is our decision. So instructions to Registrar is to ensure that the exhibits tendered by the Defence for General Talic in the early stages of this trial, until the severance of the two trials, of the two accused, will be preserved in the records of this trial and will form part of the evidence in this trial. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow, first 45 minutes hopefully we will dedicate to the conclusion of the cross-examination. I suppose there would be a short re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A short one, Your Honour, I don't think there is a great deal, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So then with the rest of the matters that you intended to deal with tomorrow, you know that roughly you have an hour less than you would have had had we finished with Mr. Dodik this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I don't think those matters will take more than an hour. It's simply some of the documents we want to put in need an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just mentioning just in case you need to discuss amongst yourselves to split the time or to organise the session. All right. I thank you and we will all meet tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
